old: Growth was not driven by commercial banks, but by the rapid emergence of microfinance mobile wallets (Floosak, mFloos) amid acute physical cash shortages.
Digital wallets represent the sole scalable vehicle for financial re-engagement in fragile settings.
Driven by urban male participation in trade, money transfers, and mobile wallet adoption for business transactions.
Gender disparity widened substantially in absolute terms over the 8-year conflict window.
Yemen maintains one of the lowest female inclusion rates globally (<4%), constrained by lack of independent ID and male guardianship norms.
Targeted gender-inclusive KYC tiers and female agent networks are urgent national priorities.
Commercial banking system experienced severe institutional contraction; zero net growth due to branch closures and frozen balance sheets.
Commercial banking sector requires balance sheet restructuring and resolution of sovereign debt arrears.
From virtually 0% in 2014 to 5.2% in 2022; fintech and microfinance bank wallet apps filled the institutional vacuum left by traditional lenders.
Evolving regulatory framework needed to interconnect mobile money switches across territorial lines.
Card issuance grew among urban salary recipients, but operational utility is crippled by non-functional ATMs and cash withdrawal caps.
Transition from magnetic stripe ATM cards to digital QR-code wallets is structurally more resilient.
Depressed due to public fears of bank insolvency, cash withdrawal limits, and negative real interest rates in hyper-inflation.
Re-establishing depositor protection funds is critical to restore confidence in formal savings.
Households shifted aggressively toward trusted community rotating savings clubs to preserve liquidity and mutual credit lines.
Fintech platforms should digitize traditional Haqba/Jam'iyya models into formal e-wallet group savings.
Banks virtually ceased retail unsecured lending; microfinance portfolios shrank due to operational risks and currency volatility.
Need first-loss credit guarantee facilities (e.g. via IFC/MIGA) to unlock bank lending to MSMEs.
Family borrowing expanded into the dominant safety net as formal wages lapsed and poverty surged above 75%.
Highlights that household survival is mediated almost entirely through social capital, not banking rails.
Local grocery store ledgers (Daftar) expanded dramatically to bridge food consumption gaps amid spiraling staple prices.
Merchant credit is the primary informal shock absorber; digitization of merchant ledgers can unlock supply-chain finance.
Massive displacement and economic collapse made domestic remittances between governorates a core survival artery.
Money Exchange Companies (MECs) established absolute hegemony over remittance distribution corridors.
Households capable of mobilizing emergency funds plummeted by nearly 16 percentage points, reflecting catastrophic buffer exhaustion.
Shock-responsive social protection must replace depleted personal buffers to prevent acute humanitarian catastrophe.
